description:
Hey! 👋 I'm Omar, a Senior Software Engineer with 5+ years of experience in React, TypeScript, Node.js, and cloud technologies. I'm passionate about AI, creativity, and turning crazy ideas into reality! 🚀

I'm leading a team at NASA Space Apps 2026, where innovation meets fun and teamwork. We're excited to collaborate with people skilled in game development, 3D design, UI/UX, storytelling, and space science.

Let's build something out of this world! 🌌
summary:
We developed The Odyssey of a Meat-a-Roid, a 3D browser game that teaches
  space mission design by letting users do it instead of reading about it.
  Raed is sent to strange planet by mistake and must build a science mission to get
  home. In a workshop market he inspects real NASA hardware, such as Dawn's ion
  thruster, the RL10 and RS-25 engines, a Voyager RTG and the SLS rockets, and
  picks a science target, instrument, engine, power source, antenna, rocket and
  orbit. Every choice changes mass, thrust, power, data and cost, and the ship
  only launches when the design works. The flight then tests it with a science
  scan, a data downlink, a dark stretch, meteoroids and a Moon-base stop. Up to
  four players share one ship, each in charge of one subsystem.

  Users rarely get to try a whole mission from concept to operation. Our game
  makes that safe: failure is explained with NASA data, players redesign and
  fly again, and the same facts are taught at three levels, from plain words to
  equations, in Arabic, English, French and Spanish.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

The Odyssey of a Meat-a-Roid is a 3D browser game in which players design, build and fly a complete science mission. Dr. Galal at Mission Control sent Raed to Strange planet by mistake. He guides Raed home by radio, but every decision is the player's.

1. Explore and repair. Raed collects water, fuel, oxygen and shield parts on the strange planet. He then repairs his wrecked ship by reading gauges to find each fault, rewiring the power bay and sorting propellants into the right tanks.

2. Design the mission. Stalls around the ship form a workshop market. The player first chooses a science target: Strange planet's rings, atmosphere, moons or tilted magnetic field. Next come instruments, memory, engine, fuel, power, antenna, shield, cabin, backup, rocket, orbit and route. Each stall shows a 3D recreation of real NASA hardware with its real facts, for example Dawn's ion thruster, the RL10C-2 and RS-25 engines, a Voyager RTG, Dawn's camera and spectrometer, and the SLS rockets.

3. Check and launch. A live ship check shows weight, engine lift, power, budget (stars), expected science data and supplies. The launch is blocked until the design works, and the game says what to fix. For example, the engine must lift the ship at Uranus's real gravity of 8.69 m/s².

4. Fly. A scan mini-game collects science data, which the player must send home using power. The crew then faces a dark stretch where sunlight is only 3.69 W/m² (0.27% of Earth's), a huge rock, a cabin emergency, a Moon-base stop for repairs and upgrades, and a meteor shower near Earth. The shower choices follow what NASA advises spacecraft operators.

5. Score and learn. The mission is scored on success, science delivered, efficiency and decisions. A report explains why it went that way, names similar real NASA missions, and shows that the player followed the same Concept Maturity Levels that JPL engineers use.

What benefits does it have?

Systems thinking. Users see a mission as one system, where a gain in one part costs something in another.

Safe failure. Every failure is explained with NASA data, and players can redesign and fly again.

Real hardware. Users learn real NASA hardware and missions: Dawn, Voyager, SLS, Webb, Cassini, Juno and Apollo 13.

Any level. Beginner uses plain words. Intermediate adds NASA's numbers. Advanced adds equations with a worked example and a practice problem.

Teamwork. 1 to 4 players share one ship, and each owns a role: propulsion, power and life support, science and data, or navigation.

What is the intended impact?

We want users, especially in Egypt and the Arab world, to understand how a real mission is designed, in their own language. The game teaches in everyday Egyptian Arabic as well as English, French and Spanish. It also introduces Egyptian scientists who work in space science: Dr. Farouk El-Baz, Dr. Essam Heggy, Dr. Tahani Amer and Ahmed Soliman. We hope teachers can use it in a single class session. Next steps are online multiplayer, more destinations and a review by experts.

What tools did we use?

Code: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Three.js r187, with no framework and no install.

Testing: Node.js tests, including checks that every equation matches NASA's published figure, and Playwright browser tests.

3D: Tripo, Blender and Mixamo, Manus AI.

Media: ChatGPT, Grok and Magnific AI and Manus AI.

AI assistants: Claude Code and Manus AI.

Hosting: Cloudflare Pages.

Repository: https://github.com/ramo772/odyssey-of-a-meat-a-roid

How is the project creative?

Choices are actions, not quiz answers. You carry parts to the ship, and they succeed or fail in flight.

Real NASA parts become game items. Each one shows its real facts next to its game stats.

Honest science. Every number is labelled as a NASA fact or a game rule. Where NASA's pages don't name a part, the game shows a "source gap" note.

Storytelling that teaches. A funny story, a monkey guide called Steve and an Egyptian-dialect script make a hard subject feel friendly.

What factors did the team consider?

Scientific accuracy. NASA values are cited, simplifications are labelled, and tests check every equation.

Different ages and knowledge levels. Three levels teach the same facts at different depths.

Language and culture. The game uses an Arabic dialect people actually speak, and players can switch language mid-game.

Access. It runs in any browser with no install, adds touch controls, lowers quality on weak computers and supports reduced motion.

Real trade-offs. There is no single correct design. A solar ship is light but must survive the dark, while an RTG never goes dark but needs a stronger engine.

Respect for real people. The scientists appear as inspiration only, with links to their NASA pages, and nothing claims NASA endorsement.
